name: First Fort Dearborn — north range (soldiers' barracks and contractor's store)
aka: Whistler's index nos. 12 and 13, 'Soldiers Barracks' and 'Contractors Store'

documented_range.note: THE RANGE IS THE FIRST FORT'S, NOT THIS COMPONENT'S. It opens on 17 August 1803, the day Swearingen's detachment reached the river at the bend where the fort was to be built (his journal, printed by Quaife), and closes on 16 August 1812, the day after the evacuation, when the fort was burned (data/exclusions.json fort_dearborn_first_1803). No source dates any single building inside it: the fort was built over the months after the arrival, and Whistler's draught of 25 January 1808 is the one day on which every component here is shown standing. It ends before the second fort's 1816 phases begin, so no scene date can resolve the two forts together.

placement.position_note: SEATED WITH ONE ORIGIN AND ONE BEARING FOR ALL FOURTEEN (T-2050), so no building moves against another. The box is the register's (data/traces/whistler_1808_fort_dearborn.json), read off the commandant's own measured draught at 4.52 px per foot from the 75 ft staff, good to about +/-1.1 ft an edge. THE ORIGIN: the staff's foot, which the register finds at the centre of the parade and within about a foot of the centre of both picket rows, is set on the fort site at local E +1152, N +221 - the Wright 1834 reading of the fort's place that docs/ROADMAP.md S5a cross-checks to 35 m against the modern landmark. That is the SITE, not the second fort's plan: John H. Kinzie (quoted on chicagology_prefire052) says the first fort 'stood upon the same ground as the last Fort' and 'was differently constructed', so the place carries over and nothing of the 1816 geometry does. THE BEARING: the frame's north is set on grid north, which is the register's own inference that the sheet's right is east, from the lake lettered down that margin; the sheet has no north arrow, so the bearing is inferred and adds nothing to it. The second fort's 8 degrees, read off Harrison 1830, is that fort's and is not borrowed. Grid and true north differ here by under half a degree. A CHECK, NOT A FIT: seated so, the outward row's west side stands about 124 ft from the 1812 river (data/terrain/epochs/e1830_natural/river.geojson) and the north-west blockhouse about 65 ft from it; the draught's red-ink '122 feet to River' from the west side and Wilson's '80 feet' from the north-west corner are figures of that size. Carry the datum's +/-20 m on the whole frame.
placement.symbolic_location: First Fort Dearborn, in the frame of Whistler's 1808 draught (register part 'north range, west room + north range, east room'): E +0.0..+24.8 ft, N +33.6..+45.6 ft of the flagstaff's foot, facing south onto the parade. SEATED (T-2050) with the whole frame: the staff's foot at local E +1152.0, N +221.0, the frame's north on grid north; this record's origin is the box's NE corner, the footprint turned 180 degrees so its front faces south.

footprint.note: MEASURED: 24.8 ft along the parade face by 11.9 ft deep — the register's two rooms, 13 (west, 11.7 ft) and 12 (east, 13.1 ft), under one roof as the draught draws them.

kind.note: Whistler's index numbers its east room 12, 'Soldiers Barracks', and its west room 13, 'Contractors Store'. Quaife: 'The building opposite was in part devoted to barracks for the soldiers and in part to housing the contractor's store of supplies'. Built as one barracks range; the store is a room and the archetype builds no interiors.

construction.note: Not stated on the sheet. Built by the garrison out of local timber in 1803; Quaife calls the factor's and agent's houses beside it 'two log houses', and the magazine is singled out as the one structure of brick.

stories.note: Whistler's index, note: 'the Barracks are two storeys high with shingled Roofs and Galliaries fronting the parade'. Quaife, reading the same sheet: 'two stories in height, with shingled roofs and covered galleries'.

wall_height_m.note: Unattested. Two storeys of log, at the second fort's inferred 5.0 m. The register refuses a height from the folded elevations, which disagree with each other by 70 percent.

roof_type.note: The index says 'shingled Roofs' and each range's elevation, folded out over the curtain, draws a pitched roof with its ridge along the range. A gable is that roof; the shingles are not a parameter the archetype reads.

roof_pitch_deg.note: Unattested. The folded elevations are not drawn at the plan scale (the register's height cross-check FAILS), so no pitch is read off them. The second fort's ranges carry the same figure.

gallery.note: The same note: 'Galliaries fronting the parade'. Built along the parade face; nothing says how deep the gallery was or how it was carried, and the archetype's gallery is a typical one.

chimneys.note: The north range's folded elevation draws one chimney above its roof, and one is built; that the drawing shows every stack is not something a folded elevation promises.

function.note: Soldiers' barracks with the contractor's store of supplies in its west room (Whistler's index 12 and 13).

officers' quarters, wood, about 30 x 60 ft, at the north-west corner (1855 caption)
parade ground 80 x 200 ft (1855 caption) AND about 80 x 400 ft (Fergus, 1850) - a disagreement, not a figure
the sutler's building (key D) and the north gate (key E)
the 1850 arrangement: quarters west of the parade ground, artillery house, barracks and storehouse east
the sun-dial on an 8-inch square timber post about 2 ft high, near the parade ground's south end (1850)
the whitewashed rough-board fence about 6 ft high, pickets already removed (1850)
the kitchen garden in the south-west corner of the enclosure (1850)
the fort's use as a general hospital from 11 July during the 1832 cholera
Bvt. Maj. Joseph Plympton arriving 1 August 1836; the soldiers withdrawn 29 December 1836
J. B. Beaubien's purchase of the reservation, 28 May 1835, for $94.61
Beaubien's later residence at the north-east corner of South Water Street and Michigan Avenue, expressly after he left the John Dean house

citations.citation: "Journal of Lieutenant James Strode Swearingen", printed as Appendix I in Milo Milton Quaife, Chicago and the Old Northwest, 1673-1835: A Study of the Evolution of the Northwestern Frontier, together with a History of Fort Dearborn (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1913), pp. 373-377. The Chicago entry, Wednesday 17 August 1803, runs across pp. 376-377.

transcribes.work: Journal of Lieutenant James Strode Swearingen, kept on the march from Detroit to Chicago in temporary command of the company sent to establish the first Fort Dearborn; entry for Wednesday 17 August 1803, the day of arrival
transcribes.note: Carries the only period measurement of the Chicago river this project has: about 30 yards wide and upwards of 18 feet deep at the fort site, a south bank about 8 feet high half a mile above the mouth, the opposite bank lower by not more than two feet BY APPEARANCES, and the banks above quite low. The last of those is the only sentence in it that reaches the modelled quadrant, and it is the one the encyclopedia paraphrase dropped. Also the pre-cut hydraulic regime in the witness's own words — 'dead water, owing to its being stopped up at the mouth, by the washing of sand' — which is why it does not license the flat surface of the 1835 scene: see docs/RESEARCH/swearingen_1803.md.

what_it_supplies: channel width and depth at the Fort Dearborn site in August 1803, from a witness standing there
the height of the south (fort) bank at that point, about 8 feet
that the north bank was lower, by an estimate made by eye and stated as a maximum of two feet
that the river above the fort had quite low banks — the only statement here about the reach this project models
that the pre-cut river was dead water, and the witness's reason for it: the mouth was stopped up by sand washing in from the lake
the distance from the fort site down to the natural mouth in 1803: half a mile
what_it_does_not_supply: any surface gradient, and therefore no evidence for or against a level water surface as a measurement
any measurement at the forks — every figure here is taken 1.2 miles downstream at the fort site
any measurement after 1803, and the 1833-34 harbour cut removed the condition the witness gives for the river standing dead
a bank height for the modelled quadrant: 'quite low' is qualitative and cannot promote a confidence
the north bank's height as a number — the 6 ft widely quoted from this passage is arithmetic performed on a hedged estimate by later writers, not a figure Swearingen wrote
any planform: the journal draws nothing and no geometry is traced from it

citations.citation: Whistler, Captain John. Original in the files of the War Department, Washington. Reproduced as the plate 'Fort Dearborn and Vicinity in 1808. From the original draft by Captain Whistler in the archives of the War Department at Washington', facing p. 164 of Quaife, Chicago and the Old Northwest, 1673-1835 (Chicago, 1913); the index is printed in full in note 413 on the same pages.
what_it_supplies: the first fort's garrison in plan at a stated scale: the double row of pickets, the two blockhouses at the north-west and south-east angles, the four barracks ranges, the magazine, two small houses, the main gate, the parade and the flagstaff
the drafter's index of 34 numbered features, and the note that two of them (the covered way and the gutters) are omitted from their places
the arrangement of the factor's and agent's establishments, stables, gardens and the houses across the river, by position only and not to scale
what_it_does_not_supply: any building height: the folded elevations disagree with each other
the fort's bearing to true north: no north arrow was found on the reproduction
the covered way to the river and the gutters, which the index itself says are omitted
anything about the second fort of 1816

research_note: THE NORTH RANGE OF THE FIRST FORT. Two numbers on the draught, one building: the contractor's store (13) is its west room and soldiers' quarters (12) its east. Between it and the north-west blockhouse stood the magazine.
